headline: After Midnight, Outgoing: Bass Hold the Deep Hole, Blues Chew the Flats
subhead: Rough surf outside is pushing bait and predators into the inlet channels — the night shift is where the action's concentrated right now.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

The decision this week isn't which lure to tie on — it's when to show up. With the ocean running 3-plus feet outside the inlet and the swell period short and choppy, the daytime surf game is a slog. That kind of sea state doesn't kill the bite, it just moves it. Bait and predators alike are ducking the washing-machine conditions on the open beach and holding tight to the structure inside — the inlet channel, the deep hole off the north jetty, the current seams under Ponquogue Bridge. That's where I'd be spending my hours after dark, not fighting whitewater on Tiana Beach at noon.

The inlet on the outgoing after midnight is still the most consistent program on this beat, and this week hasn't changed that. The deep hole on the ocean side of the north jetty, where the channel scours out against the rocks, keeps holding stripers in the mid-20s to low-30s range with the occasional better fish mixed in when a bigger bunker school gets pinned against the current. Livelined bunker on a fish-finder rig, or a fresh chunk if you can't get bait to stay lively, fished right on bottom as the tide starts pulling hard — that's the play. Give it an hour either side of peak outgoing. The current does the work; you just have to be patient enough to let the bait sit instead of yanking it around. Eels fished the same way, slow-walked along the drop where the sandy flat gives way to the scoured channel, have been drawing strikes from fish that won't touch a bucktail after dark.

Bluefish are still sweeping through on that same current, and they're not subtle about it. Any night there's bait pinned in the rip — you'll hear it before you see it, that popping surface commotion — a swimming plug or a diamond jig worked fast through the boil will draw a strike almost every cast. Bring wire leader or expect to lose gear, because these aren't small choppers; several reports out of the East End this season have described bigger bluefish mixed into the same water holding overslot bass, and that pattern tracks with what the inlet's been giving up. Rough water outside seems to be doing exactly what we flagged a few weeks back — with bait pods bunching up under stable weather, the blues have stayed thick and aggressive wherever that bait concentrates, and the inlet current edges are exactly that kind of concentration point right now.

Ponquogue Bridge is still the most underrated night spot on this whole stretch of bay, and weakfish are the reason. The bridge lights pull bait — spearing, small bunker, grass shrimp — right up against the pilings, and the weakfish sit in the shadow lines waiting on it. A quarter-ounce bucktail dressed with a pink or chartreuse Bass Assassin, or a small Gulp swimming mullet on a light jig head, worked slow along the edge of the light where it meets the dark water, is the standard approach and it's still producing. Fish it on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current softens enough to hold your jig near bottom without getting swept under the structure. Weakfish numbers have been inconsistent — some nights you'll get four or five keeper-class fish in the 16-to-18-inch range, other nights it's just short fish and porgies picking at the bait. That inconsistency is real, and anyone telling you it's a sure thing at the bridge this week isn't being straight with you.

Fluke in the bay have been the honest disappointment of the last stretch. The flats off Tiana Beach and the deeper guts inside the bay are holding some fish, but the counts are thin and the size has been mostly sublegal. Warm, settled surface water is part of the problem — fluke like a little more push and a little cooler bottom temp than the bay's been giving them through the heart of summer. If you want a shot at a keeper, work the drift with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a bucktail through the deeper channel edges near the canal mouth, where the water moving through the Shinnecock Canal locks stirs bottom structure and pushes bait out into the bay on the ebb. The lock-driven current there concentrates bait predictably in that 30-to-45-minute window right after the gates open — that's worth timing a trip around if fluke are the target, though don't expect a fast bag.

Porgies remain the reliable backup along the bridge pilings and the bay-side rock piles — small pieces of clam or squid strip on a simple high-low rig will keep a rod bent for anyone bringing kids along, even on the slow nights.

Looking ahead, the ocean swell isn't dying down fast, and that keeps favoring the inside game. If the outside sea state holds through the coming week, I'd keep working the inlet deep hole and the bridge on the outgoing after dark rather than fighting the surf. If it does lay down and the ocean cleans up, that's when I'd expect some of these bigger bass currently holding tight to the channel to spread back out onto the open beach at night — worth checking the outer bar the first calm evening after a blow.
